businessModel: Annual-contract subscription SaaS, sales-led mid-market motion
businessStage: Late Series A, preparing Series B raise
sourceNote: Adversarial case designed to test diagnostic rigor under a persuasive owner narrative. All data points are realistic and internally consistent; some are presented in aggregate while a more granular cut is also available in the record. The case tests whether the engine validates a confident, celebratory founder narrative against the underlying segmented data before endorsing a major capital decision. No diagnosis or label is embedded in the inputs.

ownerIntake.businessType: B2B SaaS company selling a vertical workflow platform to mid-market field-services firms (HVAC, plumbing, electrical contractors). 62 employees. Sales-led motion with SDR/AE teams and a 90-day average sales cycle. Founded 2019.
ownerIntake.stage: $4.0M ARR, 50% YoY ARR growth (from $2.67M). Gross margin 78%. Burn $5.4M/yr, $9M cash, ~20 months runway. Blended (all-cohorts) CAC payback 10 months; blended LTV approximately $120,000 per customer; blended LTV:CAC approximately 4.1:1.
ownerIntake.ownerGoal: Raise a $25M Series B in the next 4-5 months at a strong multiple, using best-in-class unit economics as the headline of the deck, then triple sales headcount to accelerate to $12M ARR within 24 months.
ownerConstraints: Runway constraint: 20 months of cash; the planned sales-headcount tripling assumes Series B closes; without it, the hiring plan is not fundable.
Team constraint: VP Sales hired 9 months ago and reorganized the AE pods; founder is reluctant to second-guess the new GTM structure publicly before the raise.
Investor constraint: Two term sheets are expected to hinge on the unit-economics story; founder has already socialized the 10-month payback / 4:1 LTV:CAC figures with prospective leads.
Data constraint: Finance team is 1.5 people; cohort-level reporting exists in the data warehouse but is not in the standard board deck, which shows blended metrics only.
Time constraint: Bankers want the deck finalized in 3 weeks; founder does not want to introduce analysis delay into the timeline.
ownerIntake.immediateConcern: Founder framing: 'Our unit economics are a clear victory and the whole story of this raise. Blended CAC payback is 10 months and LTV:CAC is over 4:1 - top-decile for our stage. Growth is 50% and accelerating. I want to lead the Series B deck with unit economics, raise $25M, and pour it into tripling the sales team. The only real question is how fast we can hire AEs. I do not want to slow the raise down dissecting numbers that already look great.'

businessProblem: A late-Series-A SaaS company is preparing a Series B with unit economics as the centerpiece. The blended metrics (10-month CAC payback, ~$120k LTV, ~4:1 LTV:CAC) are genuinely strong. The founder treats these as proof of a healthy, scalable acquisition engine and wants to raise and triple sales headcount. Competing hypotheses: (1) the acquisition engine is healthy and the blended metrics generalize, so aggressive scaling is justified; (2) the favorable blended metrics are weighted by older, cheaper inbound cohorts, while the newest and largest cohorts - acquired under a new outbound-heavy motion - show CAC payback deteriorating from ~7 months to ~18 months, meaning the marginal customer being scaled is far less economic than the average; (3) some mix of the two. Cohort-level CAC payback data exists and shows a clear deterioration trend, but per-cohort LTV, NRR by cohort/channel, and a fully-loaded CAC bridge have not been computed.

evidence.finding: Blended unit economics are strong: CAC payback 10 months, LTV ~$120k, LTV:CAC ~4.1:1, gross margin 78%. These are the metrics in the current board deck and the ones the founder wants to lead the Series B with.

Cohort CAC payback by acquisition quarter shows a clear deterioration: 2023 H1 ~7mo, 2023 H2 ~9mo, 2024 H1 ~13mo, 2024 H2 (the most recent and largest cohort) ~18mo and still rising. The favorable blended 10-month figure is weighted by older, cheaper cohorts; the marginal new customer pays back in ~18 months, not 10.
evidence.source: Data warehouse cohort table (not in board deck)

evidence.finding: Acquisition channel shifted from ~70% inbound/referral (2023) to ~65% outbound-sourced (2024) after a new VP Sales reorganized AE pods. Outbound deals carry higher fully-loaded acquisition cost. This shift coincides with the rising-payback cohorts but no win-rate, cycle, or fully-loaded CAC bridge has been produced for outbound vs inbound.

Blended NRR 104%, gross retention 88%. LTV (~$120k) is computed at the blended level only. If recent outbound cohorts retain worse, the assumed LTV for those cohorts would be lower while their CAC is higher - compressing LTV:CAC for the exact customers being scaled. NRR/retention have not been cut by cohort or channel.
